Pritiraj Brahma is also the author of two novels (October 2026): The Kingmaker, a political thriller (https://www.amazon.in/dp/B0HM57N18P), and The Things We Kept, a love story (https://www.amazon.in/dp/B0HM7L78H4).

# The Circuit Without the Bed — Tourism in North East India and the Capacity It Has Not Built

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-circuit-without-the-bed-northeast-india-tourism/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-11-24 · Topic: Federalism & the Northeast

North East India recorded 1.21 crore domestic and 2.21 lakh foreign tourist visits in 2023. A decade of public money has built circuits, shrines and gateways. What it has not counted is the bed, the operator and the rupee a visitor leaves behind.

ProvenancePublished 24 November 2026. Visit figures are those reported by state tourism departments and placed before Parliament in the Ministry of Tourism’s replies of 9 December 2024 and 10 March 2025; 2023 is the latest year with state-wise figures in those replies. Scheme amounts are this Review’s sums of the sanctioned and approved project costs listed in the December 2024 reply, not totals the Ministry publishes.

North East India is not short of visitors. It is short of the rooms, operators and records that turn a visit into an income.

Tourism is the industry the North East is most often told to build. Its landscapes, cultures and food are distinct, its airports have multiplied, and every state now has a tourism policy. The question this essay asks is narrower and more practical: when a visitor arrives, where does the money go, and who is building the capacity to earn it?

Four findings anchor this analysis:

- Demand is real and concentrated. The eight states recorded 1,20,78,776 domestic tourist visits in 2023, on state tourism department figures reported to the Lok Sabha on 9 December 2024. Assam’s 76,12,720 is 63 per cent of that total. Meghalaya, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh add another 37 lakh between them. Nagaland recorded 99,720 and Manipur 57,701.
- Foreign demand is small, fast-growing and narrow. Foreign tourist visits rose from about 1.04 lakh in 2022 to 2,21,050 in 2023 (Lok Sabha unstarred question 1721, 10 March 2025; the 2022 figure is this Review’s sum of the state figures). That is about 1.1 per cent of the 1.92 crore foreign tourist visits recorded across all states in 2023. Sikkim (93,908) and Tripura (66,708) account for 73 per cent of the region’s total.
- Public money has built the circuit. Swadesh Darshan sanctioned 16 projects in the region between 2014-15 and 2018-19, worth about ₹1,309 crore on the Ministry’s own project list. Swadesh Darshan 2.0 added about ₹224 crore in 2024, PRASHAD about ₹253 crore, and the 2024-25 special assistance scheme about ₹790 crore. These are roads, riverfronts, interpretation centres and gateways. They are necessary, and they are not rooms.
- Nobody publishes what the visitor spends. The official series counts visits. It does not publish nights stayed, rooms available, occupancy or spend per visitor by state. A region cannot plan hospitality investment on a count of arrivals.

## Why the bed is the binding constraint

A tourist visit becomes income only when it becomes a night, a meal and a guide. That conversion depends on private capacity: hotels, homestays, restaurants and operators who can raise capital against a predictable season. Public schemes fund the attraction. The capacity that earns from it is left to form on its own.

Three frictions slow it down. Land held under community and customary systems is hard for a lender to take as collateral, so a homestay owner struggles to borrow against the building that would earn the income. Permit regimes in several states add a step for every visitor. And connectivity still bunches demand into a few gateways and a few months. Each of these is solvable. None of them is addressed by building another gateway.

## What the circuit model measures

The schemes report what was sanctioned and what was completed. That is a record of construction. It does not say whether the new riverfront raised occupancy in the town beside it, whether homestays opened along the new road, or whether the visitor stayed a second night. In the language this Review uses elsewhere, the dashboard counts the input and leaves the outcome unrecorded.

## The counter-case, honestly stated

The circuit has to come first. Without roads, airports and sites, no investor will build a hotel, and the region’s recent gains in air connectivity are exactly the precondition this argument asks for. Counting spend is also hard where so much of the economy is informal, and a survey would cost money the states do not have.

Both points are fair. But a decade of sanctioned circuits is long enough to ask what they produced, and without a spend series nobody can answer. Infrastructure built without a measure of what it earned is a cost, not an investment.

## What we would do

- Publish a tourism ledger for each state. Rooms, occupancy, nights and spend per visitor, from an annual sampled survey, alongside the visit count.
- Tie the next tranche of circuit funding to private capacity. Release later money where homestay and hotel registrations, and lending to them, have actually grown around the funded site.
- Build a bankable tenure route for hospitality. Registered long leases from community landholders that lenders recognise, so a homestay can borrow against its own earnings.
- Make every permit digital and instant. Keep the protections the permit regimes exist for, and remove the queue.
- Sell the region by season and circuit, not by state. Visitors cross state lines; promotion and air connectivity should follow the routes they actually travel.The North East does not need to be discovered. It needs to be built for: one bed, one operator and one published number at a time. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery.

# The Platform Is the Landlord — Food Delivery, Commissions and the Economics of India’s Cloud Kitchens

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-platform-is-the-landlord-cloud-kitchen-economics/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-11-24 · Topic: Political Economy

Restaurants report paying food delivery platforms 10 to 30 per cent in commission, and up to half of what the customer paid once ads, discounts and fees are added. Two platforms hold about 90 per cent of the market. For a delivery kitchen, the rent has moved from the street to the app.

ProvenancePublished 24 November 2026. Commission and fee figures are as reported by trade and business publications between June and September 2025, citing operators, advisers and industry bodies; platforms do not publish a standard rate card, and the ranges reported differ. They are labelled as reporting throughout. Disclosure: the author is the founder of East & Ember Hospitality Group, a delivery-first food company.

A restaurant used to pay its landlord for footfall. A delivery kitchen pays the platform instead, and the platform sets the rent.

India’s food delivery market made a new kind of restaurant possible: a kitchen with no dining room, in a low-rent unit, serving customers it never meets. The model is now mainstream. This essay asks what that kitchen actually pays for its customers, and why that number decides whether the business is worth backing.

Four findings anchor this analysis:

- The commission is a range, not a rate. Reported commissions run from 10 to 28 per cent on Zomato (NDTV Profit, reported by Verdict Food Service, September 2025), 10 to 16 per cent for larger brands and above 20 per cent for smaller outlets (an Alvarez & Marsal partner quoted by YourStory, July 2025), and 16 to 30 per cent across both major platforms (Storyboard18, June 2025). Terms vary with order value, volume and brand. The small operator pays the most.
- The commission is not the whole take. Operators interviewed by YourStory described commission, advertising and discovery fees together taking 45 to 50 per cent of payouts. A restaurant-software founder quoted by Inc42 in August 2025 put the figure at 35 to 40 per cent of each transaction once logistics, payment and ad charges are counted. Visibility is increasingly bought, not earned.
- The market is concentrated, and it is being contested. Swiggy and Zomato together hold about 90 per cent of food delivery (Inc42, August 2025). Rapido’s entry offered restaurants a fixed fee of ₹25 on orders below ₹400 and ₹50 above (Storyboard18, June 2025), and Inc42 reported a government plan to commit ₹200 to 250 crore to support food delivery on ONDC.
- The platform also competes with its tenants. The National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over five lakh restaurants, has moved the Competition Commission over platforms’ own private-label food brands and their control of customer data (Inc42, August 2025).

## Why the platform is the landlord

In a dine-in restaurant, rent buys location and location buys demand. A delivery kitchen sits in a cheap unit, and its demand comes from its ranking on two apps. The commission and the advertising budget are therefore its real occupancy cost. Unlike a lease, they are variable, opaque and set by one side.

That changes what makes a delivery business investable. The useful question is not gross order value but contribution after platform costs, and how much of the customer relationship the kitchen owns. Repeat customers, a direct ordering channel and food that travels well are the delivery equivalent of a long lease.

## The counter-case, honestly stated

The platforms built this market. They pay for riders, the app and the customer acquisition no single restaurant could afford, and a 20 per cent commission is cheaper than a high-street lease in most Indian cities. Restaurants that complain about commission are often complaining about competition, and kitchens that exist only because of delivery apps have little standing to object to their price.

Much of that is true, and it is why delivery-first kitchens exist at all. But a market in which the supplier cannot see its own customer, cannot predict its own ranking and competes with the platform’s own brands is not yet a fair one. The remedy is transparency, not a price cap.

## What we would do

- Publish the full take on every order. One statement per order showing commission, advertising, discount share and fees.
- Give restaurants their repeat-customer data. At minimum, an identifier that lets a kitchen recognise and reward its own regulars.
- Separate the marketplace from the private label. Where a platform runs its own food brands, publish and audit the ranking rules.
- Fund ONDC delivery, not just onboarding. A third channel is real only when it can deliver the food reliably.
- For operators: price for the platform, build for the direct channel. Cost every dish at full platform take, and invest in the customer who will one day order direct.The delivery economy has made it cheaper than ever to open a kitchen and harder than ever to own a customer. The businesses that last will be the ones that treat the platform as a landlord to be managed, not a partner to be trusted. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery.

# The Shift Is the Contract — The Labour Codes and India’s Hospitality Employers

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-shift-is-the-contract-labour-codes-hospitality/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-11-24 · Topic: Work & Livelihoods

India’s hospitality employers asked for flexible labour law and, on 21 November 2025, got a version of it. They also got a wage definition that moves cost into benefits, gratuity after one year, and overtime at twice the rate. The industry runs on allowances, short tenures and long shifts. The codes price all three.

ProvenancePublished 24 November 2026. Provisions are as described in the Ministry of Labour and Employment’s release of 21 November 2025 and in law-firm and adviser analyses of the same date; the central rules were notified on 8 May 2026 and state rules continue to be notified. Readers should check the rules of their own state before relying on any threshold. Disclosure: the author is the founder of East & Ember Hospitality Group, a hospitality employer.

Hospitality is built on the shift. The labour codes have turned the shift into a contract with a price.

The four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025, replacing 29 central labour laws, according to the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The central rules followed on 8 May 2026, as this Review set out in Four Codes, Thirty-Six Rulebooks. For a hotel, a restaurant group or a cloud-kitchen operator, the question now is not whether the codes apply, but how they read on the floor of a kitchen at eleven at night.

Five findings anchor this analysis:

- The wage definition moves cost into benefits. Basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance now count as wages. Exclusions such as allowances and bonuses are capped at 50 per cent of remuneration, and any excess is treated as wages for provident fund, ESI, gratuity and bonus (HSF Kramer analysis). Pay structures that lean on allowances feel this most.
- Short tenure now earns gratuity. Fixed-term employees qualify for gratuity after one year instead of five, with benefits equal to permanent staff (Ministry of Labour and Employment, 21 November 2025). Seasonal and project hiring, common in resorts and banquets, now carries a deferred cost from the first year.
- The shift is regulated, and so is the overtime. Overtime is payable at twice the ordinary rate, with the worker’s consent, and work schedules must be displayed. Hours, leave and overtime apply to “workers”, which excludes managerial roles, so classifying each job is now a compliance decision.
- Night shifts open to women, on conditions. Women may work at night in all establishments, subject to consent and safety measures, alongside any state requirements that continue to apply. For kitchens and front desks that run past midnight, this widens the hiring pool and adds a transport and safety obligation.
- Thresholds favour scale. Lay-off and retrenchment without prior government approval now applies to establishments with fewer than 300 workers, up from 100, and standing orders also start at 300 (EY; HSF Kramer). In exchange, an employer contributes 15 days’ wages per retrenched worker to a re-skilling fund.

## Why hospitality feels it first

Three features of the business meet the codes head-on. Pay is built from allowances, because base wages are kept low and service charge, meals and accommodation make up the rest. Tenure is short, because the industry hires for seasons, events and openings. And the working day is long and irregular, because guests arrive when they arrive.

The codes reach each of these directly. The 50 per cent rule reaches the allowance structure, one-year gratuity reaches the seasonal contract, and double-rate overtime reaches the split shift. None of this is hostile to the industry. It does mean the cost of a hospitality job is now closer to its visible cost.

## The state is where the codes will be decided

Labour is on the Concurrent List. The central notification set the frame, but hours, leave and many thresholds take effect through state rules, and some state Shops and Establishments Acts are not superseded and may conflict with the codes (EY, November 2025). A chain operating in Karnataka, Delhi and Assam may face three readings of the same provision. Some states have floated a four-day-week option in draft rules. Flexibility will be real in some states and theoretical in others.

## Gig work reaches the kitchen door

The Code on Social Security requires aggregators, including food delivery platforms, to contribute 1 to 2 per cent of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay gig and platform workers (Ministry of Labour and Employment; EY). The levy falls on the platform, not the restaurant. But a platform sets its commission terms, and a cost it bears is a cost it will try to recover from both sides of its market. That is this Review’s analysis, not a reported figure.

## The counter-case, honestly stated

The codes may change little in practice. Much of hospitality employment sits in small, informal establishments where the old laws were also widely ignored, and a new rulebook does not by itself create an inspector. On this view the codes formalise the firms that were already formal and leave the rest untouched.

That is partly right. But the codes also make formality cheaper: one registration, one return, and social security that travels with the worker. For an operator raising institutional capital, formal compliance is not optional, and the codes lower its price.

## What we would do

- Re-cut the pay structure before the state rules land. Model every role against the 50 per cent rule and one-year gratuity, and move cost into base pay deliberately rather than by default.
- Classify every role. Draw the line between worker and managerial staff role by role, because hours, overtime and leave follow it.
- Build the night shift properly. Documented consent, transport and safety for women on late shifts, so the hiring pool widens without a compliance gap.
- Keep one compliance register per state. Update it as each state notifies its rules, and stop assuming the central rule is the operative one.
- Treat formality as an asset. Appointment letters, registered employees and clean returns are what investors’ diligence teams ask for first.Hospitality has always sold time: a night, a meal, a shift. The labour codes put a clearer price on the last of these. The employers who price it first will hire better and raise capital more easily. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery.

# The Grievance With No Address — Why India’s Students Protest at the Examination Hall

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-grievance-with-no-address/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-10-02 · Topic: Institutions & Reform

An Indian Express investigation counted 41 recruitment-exam leaks across 15 states in five years, derailing 1.4 crore applicants for about 1.04 lakh posts. Nine months after the UGC required every university to appoint a student ombudsperson, 421 had not. India’s largest student protests are not about ideology. They are about a state that runs the examination, sets the queue, and keeps no public record of either.

ProvenancePaper-leak counts are from investigative media tallies (The Indian Express, February 2024; India Today; Newslaundry; The Tribune, February 2024). They differ in period and method, and no official national series exists. Ombudsperson compliance figures are from UGC defaulter lists of January, March, June and July 2024, as reported. Graduate cohort figures are from the State of Working India 2026 (Azim Premji University).

India publishes no current national count of student protests, so the question of who protests has to be answered by what students protest about. On that the record is clear. The mobilisations that reach national scale are rarely about campus ideology. They are about examinations. An Indian Express investigation in February 2024 documented 41 leaks in recruitment examinations across 15 states in five years, governments of every party among them, derailing about 1.4 crore applicants for a little over 1.04 lakh posts. The state sets the paper, runs the hall, publishes the result and offers the job. When any link breaks, the student has nowhere to take the grievance except the street.

Students protest about many things, and some of it is politics in the ordinary sense: campus elections, national controversies, ideological contests between student wings of political parties. That protest is part of democratic life and is not the subject of this essay. The subject is the larger and steadier current: young people who have spent years preparing for an examination run by a public body, and who find that the examination was leaked, cancelled, postponed, or never completed. For that student, the protest is not a statement. It is the only way to file a complaint the state has given no other address for.

Six findings anchor this analysis:

- The largest student mobilisations are about the state as examiner and employer. The Indian Express investigation of February 2024 documented 41 leaks in recruitment examinations over five years across 15 states, affecting about 1.4 crore applicants competing for just over 1.04 lakh posts. That is roughly 135 applicants for every post whose process was disrupted. The leaks were not confined to one party’s governments.

- The wait after a failure is measured in years, not weeks. In at least 15 of the 41 cases the Indian Express examined, candidates waited nearly a year for a re-examination. In four the wait crossed two years. In seven, candidates were still waiting at the time of reporting. For an applicant near an age limit, a cancelled examination can be a lost attempt that is never returned.

- No one counts the failures officially, and the private counts disagree. India Today reported 70 leaks in seven years affecting about 1.7 crore applicants across 15 states. Newslaundry’s ten-year count identified 89 suspected cases and 48 retests affecting at least 6.5 crore candidates. The Tribune reported more than 50 cases since 2015, including 14 in Rajasthan and 14 in Gujarat. The figures differ because the periods, definitions and sources differ. That is the point: the most consequential failures of the public examination system are tallied by newsrooms, not by the state.

- The law that followed punishes cheating; it does not publish the record. The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 5 February 2024 and became law that year. It creates offences and penalties for examinations conducted by central bodies. It does not require any authority to publish, examination by examination, what was notified, held, cancelled and re-held, or how long candidates waited. Most of the documented leaks occurred in state examinations, outside its reach.

- The campus grievance office was mandated and then not staffed. The UGC (Redressal of Grievances of Students) Regulations, 2023 were notified on 11 April 2023 and required every university to appoint an ombudsperson within 30 days. In January 2024 the UGC published a list of 421 universities that had not: one central, 256 state, 162 private and two deemed-to-be universities. The list fell to 228 in March 2024, 157 by 1 June 2024, and 63 in July 2024. The naming worked. It also showed that a statutory duty was ignored for most of a year until publication made the delay visible.

- The grievance channel is built for one student at a time. The ombudsperson hears individual complaints on admissions, fees, reservation, scholarships, ragging, examinations and results. That is the right list of subjects. But a leaked paper or a cancelled recruitment cycle is a collective grievance affecting lakhs of people at once, and no institution exists to receive it, answer it, or publish what was done.

## Who protests, and about what

The student who protests over an examination is usually not a campus activist. They are an aspirant: a graduate, often in their twenties, preparing for a recruitment examination for a teaching post, a police constable’s post, a clerk’s post or a state civil service. The scale of that population is the scale of the problem. The State of Working India 2026 report from Azim Premji University puts India’s graduates aged 20 to 29 at 6.3 crore, up from 50 lakh in 1983. For a large share of them, a government post remains the most secure work available, and the examination is the only door to it.

This is why the protest so often takes the same form. It starts after a cancellation or a disputed result, moves from social media to a district headquarters or a state capital, and asks for something specific: a retest date, a published answer key, an inquiry, a relaxation of the age limit. These are administrative demands. They become political because no administrative channel exists to receive them.

## Where it happens

The map of examination protest follows the map of examination failure. The Tribune’s February 2024 count named Rajasthan, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Telangana and Uttarakhand among the states with repeated leaks in public recruitment. These are states where state recruitment boards and public service commissions run some of the largest examinations in the world by applicant count, often through private vendors for printing, logistics and online testing. The Indian Express documented papers circulated on messaging apps within minutes, papers stolen from government offices, and vendor servers allegedly compromised. Every one of those is a weak link in a chain that the state owns but does not fully control.

## How the system answers now

The present answer has three parts: cancel, investigate, re-test. Each is reasonable on its own. Together they shift the whole cost of the failure onto the candidate, who pays again in time, coaching fees, travel and age. The state’s accountability ends with an arrest. The candidate’s loss continues until a new result is published, which, in more than a third of the cases the Indian Express examined, took close to a year or longer.

National entrance tests such as NEET draw most of the attention. This essay is about the far larger number of state recruitment examinations, where the same failure has no national owner at all.

What the system does not do is publish. There is no public register where a candidate, a journalist or a legislator can see every recruitment examination in a state, its notification date, the date it was held, whether it was cancelled, why, and when the re-test took place. The information exists in every commission’s files. It is simply not assembled into the one ledger that would show which bodies deliver and which do not.

## What the future holds

Across South Asia, examination-and-jobs grievances have shown how quickly they can grow beyond the campus. India’s institutions are deeper and its federal structure spreads pressure across many capitals, so comparisons should not be pushed too far. But the underlying arithmetic is shared: a large cohort of educated young people, a public job queue that is the main route to security, and rules that many of them no longer believe are applied fairly.

The direction of the numbers matters. The State of Working India 2026 reports that graduates made up 67 per cent of unemployed Indians aged 20 to 29 in 2023, up from 46 per cent in 2017. The companion essay examines why so much of that unemployment stays out of sight. The examination hall is where it becomes visible.

## The counter-case

There is a fair argument that protest is the system working, not failing. Leaks are crimes. They are investigated, arrests follow, the 2024 Act raised penalties, and several states have legislated their own. The UGC’s own figures show compliance with the ombudsperson rule rising quickly once defaulters were named. Not every student protest is an examination grievance, and no grievance office would absorb protest that is genuinely political. On this view the state is responding, and a register adds paperwork without stopping a single leak.

The argument is half right. Enforcement matters, and naming worked for the ombudspersons. But enforcement addresses the person who leaked the paper, not the lakhs who sat it. A register would not stop a leak. It would make the cost of each one visible, attach it to a named body, and let candidates plan around a calendar the state is required to keep. That is the difference between a state that reacts to protest and one that removes the reason for it.

## What we would do

- Publish a public examinations register in every state and at the Union. For every recruitment examination, record the notification date, the examination date, the result date, any cancellation with its stated reason, and the re-test date. Publish it as open data, updated monthly. The information already sits in every commission’s files.

- Bind each recruitment cycle to a published calendar with a results deadline. A commission that misses its own deadline should have to report the reason to the legislature. A calendar the state must keep is the cheapest protection a candidate can be given.

- Return what a cancellation takes. When an examination is cancelled for a failure on the state’s side, the affected cycle should not count against the candidate’s permitted attempts or age limit, and re-test fees should be waived automatically, not on petition.

- Give collective grievances an address. Each recruitment body should have a standing grievance officer with a duty to respond publicly, within a fixed period, to any representation affecting a whole examination: answer keys, cancellations, normalisation of scores, result delays.

- Publish what the ombudspersons hear. Every university ombudsperson under the 2023 UGC regulations should file an annual return of complaints received, resolved and pending, and the median time to resolve them. Compliance with the appointment rule rose once it was published; the same discipline should apply to performance.

- Count protest by cause. State police already record public order events. A short annual statement of student agitations by cause, whether examination, fees, hostel or political, would tell governments where the grievance channel is failing before the street does.

The student outside the commission office is not asking the state for a new promise. They are asking it to finish the one it already made when it notified the examination. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery. And for this generation, delivery starts with a result that is published on the date the state set itself.

Companion essay. The same question, approached from the other side: The Unemployment Families Absorb — Why India’s Graduate Jobless Rate Stays Out of Sight.

# The Hope That Was Priced In — What Venture Capital Did, and Did Not Do, to Indian Education

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-hope-that-was-priced-in/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-10-02 · Topic: Education & Skills

Indian edtech raised about $4.1 billion in 2021 and $321 million in 2023, on Tracxn’s count. Byju’s, once valued at a reported $22 billion, entered insolvency over ₹158.90 crore owed to the BCCI. PhysicsWallah listed in November 2025 and is putting IPO money into physical centres. Venture capital brought cheap, wide access and a sales machine pointed at children. India regulates it as a consumer product, not as education.

ProvenanceFunding figures are from Tracxn’s EdTech India reports (August 2024 and as reported in 2026); Tracxn has revised its annual series between editions, and both versions are stated. Company figures are from PhysicsWallah’s offer documents as reported at listing (November 2025) and from tribunal and court records on Byju’s (NCLT, July 2024; Supreme Court, October 2024). Regulatory references are the Ministry of Education guidelines of January 2024 and CCPA guidelines of November 2024.

In 2021 Indian education technology raised about $4.1 billion, on Tracxn’s count. By 2023 the figure was $321 million. Between those two numbers sits the largest experiment India has run in letting private risk capital into the business of teaching its children. It produced something real: learning at a price far below what a family used to pay a tutor, reaching towns the old coaching industry never served. It also produced a sales machine pointed at parents, a company once valued at a reported $22 billion in insolvency over a ₹158.90 crore sponsorship debt, and a regulatory answer that treats the whole sector as a consumer-protection problem. Nobody was asked to show whether the children learned more.

Venture capital has largely not bought Indian schools, and there is a structural reason. A school in India must, as a rule, be run by a not-for-profit trust, society or company, so the equity that a venture fund buys cannot easily sit inside one. Capital therefore went to the parts of education that sit around the school: learning apps, test preparation, tutoring, and, more recently, chains of physical coaching centres. The child still attends a regulated school in the morning. Increasingly, what decides their examination result happens in the unregulated hours after it.

Six findings anchor this analysis:

- The money arrived in a single wave and left almost as fast. Tracxn’s August 2024 report records $4.1 billion raised by Indian edtech in 2021, $2.4 billion in 2022 and $321 million in 2023, an 87 per cent fall in a year. A single quarter, Q3 2021, brought $2.48 billion. Tracxn’s later series, as reported in 2026, puts 2021 at roughly $4.3 billion and 2023 at $265 million, and counts funded rounds falling from 368 in 2021 to 36 in January to August 2026. The editions differ in detail; both describe a boom and a collapse inside three years.

- The capital concentrated on school-age children and examinations. On Tracxn’s figures K-12 edtech had raised about $8 billion to August 2024, and test preparation about $7 billion. Its 2026 series puts K-12 at 51 per cent of all sector funding between 2021 and 2026. Investors were not, for the most part, funding universities or adult skills. They were funding the competition for marks and seats.

- The largest failure came through a creditor, not a regulator. On 16 July 2024 the National Company Law Tribunal admitted the BCCI’s insolvency application against Think and Learn, Byju’s parent, over unpaid dues of ₹158.90 crore. On 23 October 2024 the Supreme Court set aside the appellate tribunal’s approval of a settlement. No education authority had any formal role in the collapse of what had been the country’s most valuable education company.

- The successful model is moving offline. PhysicsWallah listed on 18 November 2025 at an issue price of ₹109. Its offer documents, as reported, showed revenue rising from ₹744 crore in FY23 to ₹1,941 crore in FY24 and ₹2,887 crore in FY25, losses of ₹84 crore, ₹1,131 crore and ₹243 crore over the same years, 4.46 million paid users in FY25, and 198 offline centres at 31 March 2025. ₹460.55 crore of the fresh issue was earmarked for new offline and hybrid centres. Public-market money is now building physical coaching capacity.

- The rules that exist are about advertising, not learning. The Ministry of Education’s guidelines of January 2024 bar coaching centres from enrolling students under 16, require tutors to be graduates, prohibit guaranteed ranks and misleading promises, and propose penalties of ₹25,000 and then ₹1 lakh before deregistration. Implementation was left to the states. The Central Consumer Protection Authority issued guidelines on misleading coaching advertisements on 13 November 2024, and by April 2025 had issued 49 notices and imposed ₹77.60 lakh in penalties on 24 coaching centres.

- No public body measures whether any of this improves learning. The school system has national learning surveys. The parallel system that families now pay for has no published outcome measure at all: not completion rates, not score improvements, not refund rates. The only numbers in the public domain are funding rounds, valuations, user counts and penalties.

## The hope

The hope was real and it should be stated plainly. Before venture-funded edtech, serious examination preparation in India meant moving to a coaching town or paying a premium in a metro. The new model put competent teaching on a phone at a fraction of that price. PhysicsWallah’s growth from a YouTube channel to 4.46 million paid users is, in part, a measure of how much unmet demand existed in towns the old industry never reached. For a family in a district headquarters, a low-cost course with a recognisable teacher is a genuine widening of opportunity.

The capital also forced the incumbents to change. Price, reach and the use of video at scale became normal in a sector that had been local and expensive. Whatever happens to individual companies, that shift is unlikely to reverse.

## The scare

The scare is in what the money was paid to maximise. Venture capital rewards growth, and in education growth means enrolling more children, earlier, at higher lifetime value. The Ministry’s January 2024 guidelines exist because the government received complaints about student suicides, fire incidents, poor facilities and teaching practices in coaching centres. The under-16 bar is a direct response to the push to enrol children younger. The CCPA guidelines exist because guaranteed ranks and selective use of toppers’ photographs had become a standard selling tool.

The Byju’s collapse showed a second risk. When a venture-funded education company fails, the people exposed are not only its investors and lenders but families who paid in advance for courses, and employees owed wages. The insolvency process is designed to rank creditors, not to protect a child’s course of study. There is no education regulator with a duty to step in.

## Why the regulator is a consumer authority

India’s education law regulates institutions: a school is recognised, a university is created by statute, a college is affiliated. A learning app is none of these. A coaching chain is a business. So the state reaches the sector through the instruments it has, which are consumer protection, advertising standards and, when a company fails, insolvency law. Each treats the student as a customer. None asks what was learned.

The shift offline makes this gap more consequential, not less. A physical coaching centre with hundreds of students in a building is exactly what the January 2024 guidelines were written for, and their force depends on each state adopting them. A national company now opens centres faster than many states have notified rules to govern them.

## The counter-case

The strongest argument against regulating further is that the market has already disciplined the sector. The funding collapse punished the companies that grew without a business model. The survivors are leaner, cheaper and closer to what families want. PhysicsWallah’s losses fell from ₹1,131 crore to ₹243 crore in a year; a listed company publishes audited accounts and answers to a securities regulator. Adding an education regulator on top, the argument runs, would raise costs and price out exactly the low-income students the model reached.

Much of that is right, and nothing here argues for licensing teaching. But market discipline measures whether a company makes money, not whether a child learns. A securities filing discloses revenue and paid users; it does not disclose how many students finished a course or improved a score. The gap is not regulation of price or entry. It is the absence of any published outcome, which is the one thing a family cannot find out for itself before paying.

## What we would do

- Publish an outcome disclosure for every registered coaching provider above a size threshold. Completion rates, refund requests and refunds paid, and, where a provider advertises results, the denominator: how many students enrolled for every one whose result is advertised. The CCPA guidelines already restrict how results are shown; this would require them to be shown honestly.

- Protect advance fees. Above a defined amount, fees paid in advance for a course should be held in a protected account or covered by insurance, so that a provider’s insolvency does not take a family’s money with it. Families are among the most exposed creditors in an education company collapse and currently have no special standing.

- Finish adoption of the 2024 coaching guidelines in every state, with a public tracker. The Ministry of Education should publish which states have notified binding rules, which have not, and how many centres are registered in each. National chains open centres in every state; the floor should be the same in every state.

- Bring large offline coaching centres under the school safety regime. Fire safety, building occupancy, counsellor access and the mental-health duties the Supreme Court set in July 2025 should apply to a coaching centre with hundreds of students exactly as they apply to a school of the same size.

- Measure the shadow system. Add questions on paid coaching, by type and spend, to the national household and learning surveys, so that the state can see how much of a child’s education now happens outside the school and whether it is closing or widening gaps.

Venture capital did not create the demand for coaching. It found it, priced it, and briefly bet that it could grow without limit. The demand outlasted the bet. The task now is to make sure the next wave is judged on what reaches the child, not on what the funding round announced. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery. In education, delivery is the only number that should ever have been priced in.

Companion essay. Read alongside Where the Seats Came From — Private Supply and the Regulator That Did Not Follow.

# The Platform Is Not the Payroll — India’s Gig Workforce and the Protection It Was Promised

URL: https://www.pritirajbrahma.in/review/the-platform-is-not-the-payroll/
Author: Pritiraj Brahma
Published: 2026-10-02 · Topic: Work & Livelihoods

NITI Aayog estimated 77 lakh gig workers in 2020-21 and projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30. The Code on Social Security recognises them. By August 2025 the Ministry of Labour counted over 3.37 lakh registered as gig or platform workers on e-Shram, against a government estimate of more than one crore. For many young Indians the platform is where work exists. The state has written their protection into law and not yet found them.

ProvenanceWorkforce estimates are from NITI Aayog’s report on the gig and platform economy (June 2022, via PIB) and later government estimates for 2024-25 as reported. e-Shram registration figures are from a Ministry of Labour and Employment statement (3 August 2025) and later counts as reported in 2026; the series differ and are stated separately. Legal references are the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Union Budget 2025-26.

NITI Aayog estimated that 77 lakh people worked in India’s gig economy in 2020-21 and projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30. The Code on Social Security, 2020 was the first Indian law to name gig and platform workers and promise them a social-security scheme. Five years on, the Ministry of Labour’s own count in August 2025 was over 3.37 lakh gig and platform workers registered on the e-Shram portal, against a government estimate of more than one crore in the sector. For a large share of young Indians who cannot wait for a matched job, the platform is where work exists. The state has written their protection into law. It has not yet found most of the people it is meant for.

This Review has argued that graduate unemployment in India is carried by families who can afford to let a child wait. The other half of that argument is what happens to young people whose families cannot. They take the work that is available, and for a fast-growing share of urban youth that work is mediated by an app: delivery, ride-hailing, home services, warehouse shifts. It is counted as employment. It is not a payroll, and the protections attached to a payroll do not follow it.

Six findings anchor this analysis:

- The workforce is large and growing quickly from a small base. NITI Aayog’s June 2022 report estimated 77 lakh gig workers in 2020-21, 2.6 per cent of the non-agricultural workforce and 1.5 per cent of all workers. It projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30, or 6.7 per cent of the non-agricultural workforce. The share of gig workers in total workers rose from 0.54 per cent in 2011-12 to 1.33 per cent in 2019-20.

- It is not only low-skilled work. NITI Aayog found about 47 per cent of gig work in medium-skilled jobs, 22 per cent in high-skilled and 31 per cent in low-skilled, with the medium-skilled share falling and both ends rising. The platform economy is absorbing graduates as well as early school-leavers.

- The law recognises the worker; the scheme depends on rules and registration. The Code on Social Security, 2020 defines gig and platform workers and allows the Union to frame schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits and old-age protection, funded in part by a contribution from aggregators of 1 to 2 per cent of turnover, capped at 5 per cent of payouts to workers. Access to any such scheme runs through registration.

- Registration is a fraction of the estimated workforce, and the counts disagree. The Ministry of Labour stated that as of 3 August 2025, more than 30.98 crore unorganised workers had registered on e-Shram, including over 3.37 lakh gig and platform workers. The government’s own estimate for the sector in 2024-25 was more than one crore. Later reporting put gig registrations at about 8.58 lakh by January 2026 against a NITI Aayog estimate of 1.27 crore for 2024-25, and at roughly 12 lakh by mid-2026 after an aggregator registration drive. On every count, most of the workforce is not yet visible to the scheme meant to cover it.

- The Union Budget moved, but on health cover, not income. The Union Budget 2025-26 announced registration of online platform workers on e-Shram, identity cards, and health cover under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, which provides up to ₹5 lakh per family per year for hospitalisation. That is meaningful protection against one kind of shock. It does nothing for income lost to an account deactivation, an injury that stops work, or a fall in rates.

- The workers have begun to organise on their own. A nationwide strike by gig workers on New Year’s Eve 2025, following a token strike on 25 December, disrupted deliveries in several cities and drew attention to hours, pay and the absence of grievance channels. When an institution does not exist to hear a collective grievance, it surfaces on the street, as it does in recruitment examinations.

## Why the platform is where young people land

The platform offers what the formal labour market does not: immediate work, no interview, no degree requirement, and pay the same week. For a young person whose family cannot finance a long job search, that is decisive. It is also why the headline unemployment rate stays low. A graduate who drives for a ride-hailing app while preparing for an examination is employed in the survey’s terms, and the companion essay explains why that matters.

The trouble is not that the work exists. It is that it carries none of the attachments that let work become a career: no provident fund, no employer health insurance, no maternity cover, no record of experience that another employer recognises, and no route to a grievance officer. The work pays today and accumulates nothing for tomorrow.

## The registration problem

India chose to deliver gig-worker protection through a national registry of unorganised workers, e-Shram, launched in August 2021. As a database of the unorganised workforce it has been a large achievement: more than 30 crore registrations. As a route to gig-worker protection it has so far reached a small minority. Self-registration asks a worker to identify as a gig or platform worker, and many do not, or register under another category. Aggregator registration, where platforms upload their workers, is the more reliable route and has started only recently.

The disagreement between counts is itself the finding. When the Ministry’s own figure, the sector estimate and later reported counts differ by factors of three or more, no one can say what share of the workforce is covered. A scheme that cannot count its beneficiaries cannot be held to a coverage target.

## The counter-case

There is a serious argument for leaving the platform model largely alone. Flexibility is the point: many workers want hours they control and several apps at once, and a regime that pushed platforms towards treating them as employees could shrink the very work that gives young people an entry. Rajasthan, Karnataka and others have legislated their own welfare frameworks, and the Union has extended health cover. On this view the system is evolving at a sensible pace, and heavier obligations would raise prices and cut jobs.

Flexibility is worth protecting, and nothing here argues for converting gig workers into employees. But portable protection does not require employment status. A contribution from aggregators is already in the law. The question is whether it reaches the worker. Registration is the bottleneck, and it is a delivery problem, not a design one.

## What we would do

- Make aggregator registration the default, and publish the count monthly. Every platform above a size threshold should upload its active workers to e-Shram as a condition of operating, with a single published monthly figure for registered gig and platform workers, by state and by platform category.

- Collect and publish the aggregator contribution. The Code provides for a contribution of 1 to 2 per cent of turnover, capped at 5 per cent of payouts. Publish how much has been collected, from how many aggregators, and what it has been spent on.

- Add income protection to health cover. Health insurance under PM-JAY covers hospitalisation. Add an accident and income-loss benefit funded from the aggregator contribution, so that an injury that stops work does not also stop income.

- Give every platform worker a grievance address. Require each platform to name a grievance officer, publish a response timeline for deactivations and payment disputes, and report the number of grievances received and resolved each quarter.

- Make gig experience count. Let a worker draw a verified record of hours and ratings from each platform into a portable credential, so that years of work become evidence another employer can recognise. For young workers, that is the difference between a job and a beginning.

India has done the harder intellectual work: it has named the gig worker in law and accepted that protection should follow the worker rather than the employer. What remains is the ordinary work of delivery, which is finding the worker, collecting what the law already provides for, and paying it out. Politics is the promise. Governance is the delivery. For a generation that starts its working life on an app, delivery means the platform is a first job, not the only one.

Companion essay. The same question, approached from the other side: The Unemployment Families Absorb — Why India’s Graduate Jobless Rate Stays Out of Sight.
